summary: A memo by John McCarthy on how documents with arbitrary characters could be stored, shown, edited and printed on any equipment. It reviews where things stood: 96-character ASCII, many sites on 64-character sets, and Stanford's larger character set. It then proposes how to move toward a larger shared set, with special reference to the ARPANET.

eli5.summary: Different computers know different letters, so some cannot show certain symbols. This note asks how all machines could share a bigger alphabet so everyone can read each other's documents.

questions: how to share character designs across networks
subtitle: A proposal for sharing documents with arbitrary symbols across the ARPANET.

tldr.problem: Different computers use different character sets, so documents with uncommon symbols cannot be reliably displayed or printed on all equipment.
tldr.mechanism: Establish a registry of characters with unique 17-bit numbers and 50 by 50 dot matrix designs, and a registry of character sets that map local codes to registered characters. Documents state their character code; devices convert descriptions to their own format.
tldr.outcome: Once the registries exist and devices implement conversion software, documents can be exchanged across machines with different keyboards, displays and printers.

today: RFC 373 is Unknown status. The proposal anticipated Unicode and font rendering by decades. Modern systems use Unicode, which assigns multi-byte code points to characters, and rely on font files rather than centralized dot matrices.

sections.title: The Character Set Problem
sections.content: In 1972, computers had incompatible character sets. Some machines only supported 64 characters (no lowercase letters), while others had 96-character ASCII. Stanford had built its own 114-character set. John McCarthy's memo asks how devices with different character generators could reliably exchange documents containing arbitrary symbols.
sections.eli5: Each computer has its own alphabet. Some have only uppercase, some have 96 characters, and Stanford built its own set with more. The problem: a document typed on one cannot be read the same way on another.

sections.title: The Registry Solution
sections.content: McCarthy proposes two registries. The character registry gives each character a unique 17-bit number (enough to include Chinese), an ASCII name, and a picture on a 50 by 50 dot matrix. The character set registry maps local bit sequences to registered character numbers. A document states its character code, either by name or with a header table and escape characters.
sections.eli5: Make a big library of all possible characters with pictures. Each character gets a number. Then, documents just say which characters they use, and what numbers on that computer mean which library characters.

sections.title: Device Support
sections.content: Different devices—printers, displays, terminals—render characters differently. Programmers supporting each device can either manually create files mapping registered descriptions to device-specific formats, or write programs to convert from the dot matrix to their device's method. Line printers are easiest because they can load character designs at job start. Displays with per-unit memories work similarly. Displays sharing a character memory require more complex management to keep frequently used characters in memory.
sections.eli5: A printer or screen can pick which characters it knows, load them when needed, and show them its own way. Devices that share a picture memory have to be more careful not to run out of space.
